caption:
Summer's Over... Time to Store It Securely

As summer comes to an end across Prince Edward Island, many people are storing their boats, trailers, ATVs, personal watercraft, lawn equipment, and other seasonal gear.

Before you put it away for the season, take a few simple steps to help protect your property from theft:

✅ Lock boats, trailers, and equipment whenever possible
 ✅ Store items in a secured building or well-lit area
 ✅ Use hitch locks, wheel locks, or chains on trailers
 ✅ Record serial numbers, make, model, and identifying features
 ✅ Take clear photos of your property and keep the information in a safe place
 ✅ Install security cameras or motion-activated lighting if available
 ✅ Remove valuables, keys, and electronics from boats and vehicles
 ✅ Consider GPS tracking devices for high-value equipment
 ✅ Report suspicious activity to police right away

Taking a few minutes now could save you a lot of frustration later.

If theft does occur, having photos and serial numbers can greatly assist police in identifying and recovering stolen property.

#PEIRCMP #CrimePrevention #ProtectYourProperty #BoatSafety #CommunitySafety #PEI

Bookmark Readerity Talk & Soirée is TONIGHT and the chapbook is in and looks beautiful! Everyone who comes this evening, will receive a copy.  We hope you can come and enjoy an evening of stimulating conversation with other book people. The highlight of the evening will be this year’s Readerity Talk by award-winning author Carol Bruneau who will be in conversation with Deirdre Kessler

Time: 7 pm
Location: Studio 1, Confederation Centre of the Arts
Tickets: Free, all are welcome

We are honoured to welcome Nova Scotia author, Carol Bruneau as this year’s Readerity author with her brilliant contribution, Finding One’s Place in the Land of Strange: Carlo Collodi’s The Adventures of Pinocchio: Story of a Puppet.
 
When asked how the rereading of Pinocchio for Readerity gave her insight into the social and political times in which we now live, Carol said she had “no idea when she chose to reread Pinocchio that the story would reflect so eerily on conditions now. Social injustice, the suffering of the poor, the immorality of the greedy, the evils of a transactional world rife with grifters - the book has it all, as if tailored for readers in the times we find ourselves in. And yet goodness and love endure, even when at times they feel like feeble flames in the darkness. In Collodi’s story, even the most blockheaded puppet eventually evolves into a human, at the core of whom is a beating, loving heart.”

caption:
Stories of the Studio

And Just Like THAT It’s Fall

As we always say first thing in the morning “It’s going to be a GREAT DAY!

And it always is. It’s only 4:00pm and the day has flown by with many things accomplished!  

The Studio and Gallery look very sleepy and quiet from looking at the building but behind closed doors, Robert is waking up the studio by many different jobs today!

Phoenix our little kiln is just NOT a pretty face! She did a bisque last night and still hot enough to keep are coffees warm this morning 

Robert will be unloading her and then reloading her for a firing when big DraGON is done! Robert fully loaded him this morning with all kinds of soup latte in Swirl and a few Badlands 

We have 7 Swirl large vases and 4 in Badlands design so these are the first vases in this design so we are anxious to see how they will look!
EXCITING! 

I’ll keep you posted!!!

We have not seen those Swirl vases since the summer in early August so it will be lovely to have a few new vases the gallery to go along with our little Sand Dune vases!

It wasn’t long before we did a tour apt. for a couple going off Island. It was lovely to show Yvonne and Andre from Maine how the magic is all done! So a couple of Robert’s mugs and one of my hummingbird tiles will be going over to Maine with them  Thank you for your support of the craft, You two!❤️

After our company left Robert stayed to glaze and I quickly dunked a few of my ornaments for DraGON before Robert closed up the lid.

Quickly I ran in to Charlottetown to get my haircut done at Magicuts by my favourite girl Mihoko! We always have such a great time! And she did a great job!
She always makes me look and feel good and I’ll be already when we open up Saturday and Sunday! 
❤️✂️
Thanks Mihoko I love the way you cut my hair! You always get it right!

Then I was off to get pumpkins and gourds for the front of the shop. Just like that our summer was gone and now we are into the fall!
How did THAT happen so quick?

Still a beautiful season and a great time to get out and see nature’s beauty!

The yard looks lovely with the new fall decorations so if you are out this way on the Green Gableshore: Kensington, Stanley Bridge, New Glasgow, Rustico (North, South/Central) Cavendish Drive, make sure you take a stop in this weekend to 17 Broadway Road, Hope River, PEI

We are off of the St. Mary’s Road that runs between Stanley Bridge and New Glasgow! You’ll see the Robert McMillan Pottery blue government signs and also you will see our colourful Poppies Porch Chairs at the end of the drive by our sign.

Please feel free to stop in. Take a tour on the Studio floor and see where and how Robert McMillan makes and applies his multilayers of glazes! 

His pottery is microwave and dishwasher safe. Made by his hands for your hands! Handles that will hold your hand, perfectly! Come try one out!

The Gallery will be full of pretty items and if you are looking to buy that special gift or pre-Christmas order, this might be you new go to, pottery shop where you get to know your potter! 

We want our gallery ti be your new place to BE, have fun and enjoy an experience! ❤️

I’ll keep you posted with DraGONs opening when it happens -should be late tomorrow night! ❤️ and the colours amazing! 

You can also take advantage of our beautiful photo screen to get a great family/friends fall photo! Always a fun time ❤️

So come meet your potter and the Potter’s Wife of Hope River and join our fun filled gallery of music, laughter, stories and being social. We love our visitors so pop on by!

We’ll be seeing you soon

caption:
Growing up in New Dominion, there were no apples orchard near us but my sister and I had a few wild trees that we would get a sour snack from. 
   Our Nan and Pop would some times take us apple picking in Tryon, at the farm of Betty and Everett Howatt. 
   Betty and Everett were a special breed. Community leaders, environmentalists and renowned farmers, who operated Willowshade Farms for over 50 years, a farm that had been settled by their family, over 200 years prior. 
   The trees were large and we relished the chance to climb a ladder, to pick the delicious fruit, knowing that my Grandfather was behind us to ensure our safe endeavors and our Grandmother was watching, waiting to turn our prizes into pies and sauce, for the coming winter.
   It was a social outing and my Grandparents seemed to know everyone, stopping frequently to talk with other pickers. My pop always made a habit of talking to Everett, as he must have known him. In those days, of tight communities and smaller family farms, the harvest was always in the conversation and news of "the crop", traveled far and wide, on the tongues of the rural population. 
   Speeding ahead 20 years, there I was. Just out of the Culinary Institute, with a piece of land and an idea. It was 1988 and I was looking for a way to farm my land. 
   Leaning on my memories and with my father having a small orchard in West Prince, I decided that growing apples, was the way to grow. It was social. It was environmentally sustainable and it filled a need in me, to produce a product. Not just grow food but make something that was high quality and nutritious.
    That's where the idea for a Upick and Cider Orchard took root. Varieties were chosen for their unique flavors, blending sweet and sharp notes, with tart and spices, to make a premium flavored drink that would stand out, among other ciders. 
   We haven't stopped. Although we have planted some more modern varieties in the last several years, we have also planted some gastronomic types, that will allow us to take our adventure to the next level and we look forward to the future, experimenting with flavors, to bring even more taste to the market.
   Being a cider orchard, means that we can leave our trees to grow to their potential, reduce our use of pesticides and have a blend of larger and smaller apples, growing along side each other, to suit different needs. 
   Our orchard offers a more tranquil, sheltered and whimsical experience, where a family, a group of friends or a couple on a date, can find quiet and privacy, to enjoy their own company and the opportunity to gather, share their time and make some lasting memories, as my sister and I did, so many years ago.

Bringing Indigenous health education to the community 

❤️ This fall, third-year nursing students at UPEI are getting the opportunity to learn about Indigenous health, healing and well-being directly within our Mi’kmaq community here in Epekwitk.

 Through the “NURS 3250: Indigenous Health, Healing and Wellbeing” course, students will learn from the knowledge and experience of Abegweit community members, guided by Dr. Terry LeBlanc and members of the Abegweit Health Centre.

 The course was developed as a response to Truth and Reconciliation Commission Call to Action #24, helping future health professionals build a deeper understanding of Indigenous health and culturally safe care.

 We’re proud to work with UPEI to support opportunities that bring education, community and Indigenous knowledge together.

caption:
⭐️Summer Student Employment Highlight ⭐️

Meet Ronald (Ron) Lanngren, a member of Abegweit First Nation, who started working at the Abegweit Hatchery at the end of June. The hatchery supports biodiversity and conservation efforts and is currently c growing approximately 7,000 Atlantic brook trout. The team also works with striped bass, Atlantic salmon, and eel. 

Ron, who heads into Grade 12 at Morell High School this fall, cleans tanks and helps with feeding. Since he lives on reserve, he can get to the hatchery for weekend feedings when needed, making it a great fit. He enjoys the easygoing  pace, the quiet environment, and working with his hands.

Ron works under Brezlyn Knockwood, the hatchery technician. Brezlyn has been teaching Ron to be a good steward to the animals in their care, following a "fish come first" philosophy. Ron is learning fish identification, biology, life cycles, and how to spot changes in behaviour, along with the note-taking side of aquaculture and the accountability and responsibility that comes with caring for living creatures. He's also learning about Indigenous species and the Mi'kmaq's cultural connection to fish and their environments, and how Indigenous people have historically led the way in conservation and ecological stewardship.

 It's all new territory for Ron, who didn't grow up around fish and had never been fishing, something Brezlyn is set to change by taking him out for a bass fishing experience during his final week on the job!

 Thank you to the team at the Abegweit Hatchery for being such great mentors this summer, and congrats to Ron on a job well done!
